Computer scientist Scott Aaronson says he has heard multiple rumors that OpenAI or Anthropic, or both, have discovered a polynomial-time algorithm for integer factorization.

Ledger’s CTO has now confirmed hearing similar rumors surrounding three major cryptographic breakthroughs at frontier AI labs:

• INTEGER FACTORIZATION IN P: A sufficiently efficient algorithm would break RSA encryption without requiring a quantum computer, threatening banking systems, government communications, digital authentication, software signing and much of the world’s digital infrastructure.

• ELLIPTIC CURVE CRYPTOGRAPHY (ECC): Bitcoin does not rely on RSA but instead relies on elliptic curve cryptography for its digital signatures. A practical breakthrough here could allow attackers to derive Bitcoin private keys from exposed public keys and steal funds using ordinary computers. Bitcoin’s SHA-256 hashing and proof-of-work mining would not necessarily be compromised.

• RING-LWE: A breakthrough undermining its quantum resistance could compromise a major mathematical foundation of post-quantum cryptography, jeopardizing parts of the world’s ongoing migration to quantum-resistant systems.

Unlike quantum computing, an efficient classical attack on RSA or ECC could potentially be distributed as software and executed on conventional computers worldwide.

Perhaps the bigger concern is what such discoveries would reveal about AI’s ability to solve foundational mathematical problems that have resisted decades of human research.

Ledger’s CTO remains skeptical that any of these cryptographic primitives have been completely broken but acknowledges that responsibly disclosing such a discovery without triggering mass exploitation would be extremely difficult.

All three rumors remain unverified.

items.content:
Yes, actually a bunch of them. Apart from efficiency gains, self-coordination among agents, in a swarm  increases coverage by a lot.

For e.g, I published a benchmark last month (https://t.co/8r4RbFKNZh) where I compared models from all leading labs (including open-weight models) against an application containing 60+ complex vulnerabilities. Back then, none of the open-weight models performed well, and they were far behind frontier models.

Over the last few weeks, I have been tweaking different combinations of swarms, some inspired by nature (like how ants, bees, bird flocks & fish schools coordinate) and some very simple ones using an append only message board. 

i observed that, by using only open-weight models in a self-coordinated swarm with a shared message board where they collaborate (and using the combinations I mentioned above), while also letting some agents work blindly (because n agents starting with the same prompt will produce n different results), I was able to achieve near-frontier-level recall on some tasks. The coordination among them acted as a multiplier for the vulnerabilities they discover, and it was 2x-5x result sometimes in terms of no of vulns discovered.

So yeah, something we expected might now actually happening.

RT @HackingLZ: A good chunk of the cybersecurity industry exists because of insecure code, insecure defaults, and decades of technical debt.

Models should be generating secure code by default, not double dipping on tokens to go back and secure the code they just generated.

Much of what we deal with today stems from legacy systems and backwards compatibility. Windows is a prime example of the security challenges that come with decades of supporting legacy functionality.

If we’re heading towards a world where it costs more to secure software than the value that software delivers, there’s a fundamental economic imbalance.

The goal should be to reduce the cost of security through better engineering, not turn security into a bigger industry than the thing it’s protecting.

items.content:
Someone who read the deck told me this was the most important slide for them, because they hear the same thing all the time: the attackers use AI, so the defenders should just use AI too.

If they attack us with fire, why not defend with fire? Because you can burn yourself.

The asymmetry isn't in the technology. It's in what a mistake costs. An attacker's agent can pick the wrong exploit, look at the error and try another route. It only needs one to work. Once a defender's agent is allowed to isolate hosts, kill processes or disable accounts, every wrong call can become a production incident, even when no attacker is there.

That doesn't mean AI has no place in defense. It can move fast where a mistake is cheap: correlating telemetry, rebuilding timelines, collecting evidence, searching other systems for the same traces. A wrong guess there costs an unnecessary query. For actions that change production, I'd keep the agent that reasons apart from the component that is allowed to act, and decide in advance which actions are safe enough to run on their own.

I think automated response will come, first where the consequences are clear. Until then, the attack surface has to shrink.

I wrote about this in more detail in August:
https://t.co/F3ciMHYJlP

3 pieces of advice I’d give to every founder:
